Lessons.Title: Solving Systems by Elimination (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: explain why combining two true equations produces another true equality at the system's solution, and solve a contextual system through addition or subtraction. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L15, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/15/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Addressing HSA-REI.C.6; Building Towards HSA-REI.C.5. The source emphasizes logical justification of elimination, not a memorized rule alone.

Original bookshop model: two notebooks and one pen cost $11 (2n+p=11); one notebook and one pen cost $7 (n+p=7). Subtract the second equality from the first: n=4, then p=3. This subtraction is valid because the same combination of quantities is subtracted on both sides; the pair must satisfy both original prices.

Alternate original system x+y=10 and 2x−y=8 has opposite y coefficients. Adding gives 3x=18, x=6, y=4. Explain in words why a shared solution of both is guaranteed to satisfy the sum equation, but why an arbitrary solution of the sum need not satisfy the whole system.

Partner task: write and justify an addition proof and a subtraction proof; critique a calculation where only left sides were combined, and verify solutions with arithmetic and a shared coordinate graph. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correct elimination, justification of equal additions, verified pair, and contextual/graph interpretation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equalities can be combined
KeyConcepts.Definition: If two equalities are true for a pair, the sum or difference of their sides is also equal.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Combine both sides term by term.

KeyConcepts.Title: Elimination and back-check
KeyConcepts.Definition: The cancellation reduces the system to one unknown but doesn't replace all original constraints.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Substitute the result into an original equation.

KeyConcepts.Title: A sum equation is necessary but not sufficient
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every common solution satisfies a sum, but an arbitrary sum-line point might not satisfy both originals.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Retain at least one original equation for verification.
KeyConcepts.Example: x=6 alone from 3x=18 doesn't yet determine y.

WorkedExamples.Title: Subtract two purchase equations
WorkedExamples.Question: 2n+p=11, n+p=7.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: Subtract full second equation from first.

WorkedExamples.Title: Add equations with opposite signs
WorkedExamples.Question: x+y=10, 2x−y=8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain why one sum is insufficient
WorkedExamples.Question: Does (6,9) solve the sum 3x=18, and the system x+y=10,2x−y=8?
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: The sum equation alone contains extra points.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; (6,9) is not a system solution.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The equation equality is then destroyed.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add or subtract both right sides too.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Not checking the pair after elimination
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A sum line admits many non-system solutions.

SummaryPoints: Add or subtract equalities to eliminate a variable.
The common pair remains a solution of each combined equation.
The result of elimination still requires an original equation for a full solution.
Teacher assesses the reasoning and contextual explanations.
